35.usefulness: The strongest methodological fit for the deployment-density half of our project, and the only one of the four that comes with runnable code: all data and scripts are on GitHub at https://github.com/DzhZzz/Data-Driven-Sparse-Sensing.git. The accuracy-versus-sensor-count curve is exactly the deliverable SA Water would find actionable, and QR pivoting is cheap enough that we could produce it within a semester. The evaluation design is worth copying wholesale: benchmarking against both an exhaustive optimum and random Monte Carlo placement is what separates a defensible recommendation from an arbitrary one, and the noise and dropout experiments give us a ready structure for a robustness section. The dropout regression is the most transferable idea in the paper: sensor criticality is explained not by QR selection order (adjusted R-squared of only 0.159) but mainly by maximum modal loading, with redundancy and matrix conditioning adding more; that gives us a principled way to tell SA Water which sensors need redundancy. The related work section is also a useful bibliography, and Crowley et al. (2025) on information-theoretic sensor placement for large sewer networks looks worth adding to our reading list.
35.limitations: The node-level results are substantially weaker than the abstract or headline figure suggests, and this matters for a utility that cares about specific locations rather than aggregate accuracy. The first-quartile node-level NSE falls to -1.354 at four sensors, with 52.6% of nodes below 0.5; even at ten sensors 6.6% of nodes remain below 0.5 and 2.6% below zero. System-oriented placement does not deliver spatially uniform accuracy. The authors are equally frank that the SWMM model was never validated against field measurements because no monitoring data exist, so it is described as a physically grounded scenario generator rather than a calibrated digital twin; that circularity is the framework's foundational weakness, since sensor locations are chosen to reconstruct simulated flows. Their own uncertainty test confirms the concern in a specific way: reconstruction accuracy is robust across nine perturbed SWMM variants, but the selected sensor locations are not, with 67% of variants showing low Jaccard overlap at six sensors and 22% still low at ten. In other words the method reliably works, but which nodes it picks depends on how the model was parameterised. DSS is also fundamentally linear, so it misrepresents threshold-driven overflow nodes that sit at zero until activated, producing spurious weak flows or missed activations. Only one variable (flowrate) is handled, there is no forecasting capacity, and the single catchment is small, single-outlet stormwater rather than sanitary sewer. It remains a preprint under review at Water Research.
35.conclusions: System-level NSE rose from 0.896 at one sensor to 0.993 at ten across the five observed events, and from 0.842 to 0.994 for the 200-year design storm; three sensors already reach a mean of 0.949 and performance is near-stationary above 0.982 from five sensors onward. DSS tracks the exhaustive optimum closely for one to four sensors, with mean gaps of 0.002 to 0.013, and consistently beats random placement, whose distribution is heavily tailed into strongly negative NSE. Multiplicative Gaussian noise up to 15% has almost no effect. Single-sensor dropout matters, but unevenly: at six sensors, removing three of them costs 0.358, 0.219 and 0.335 NSE while the other three cost almost nothing; at ten sensors, vulnerability concentrates in two locations. Mean dropout loss falls with density (0.476 at two sensors to 0.090 at ten) but worst-case loss stays high (0.623 to 0.367). Failure impact is best explained by modal loading (64% of explained variance), then QR rank (22%), conditioning (7%) and redundancy (6%).
35.reflection: Having read the full text, my earlier read was too optimistic. The headline of three sensors at NSE 0.949 is a system-level average that hides a long tail of poorly reconstructed nodes, and the model-uncertainty test shows that the specific locations, which is what a client actually installs, are the least stable part of the output. For our project that suggests a specific framing: DSS is a strong tool for answering how many sensors are enough and for producing a defensible density curve, but weaker for asserting that these exact manholes are the right ones. If SA Water's hydraulic model is uncalibrated, we should say plainly that location recommendations carry more uncertainty than the reconstruction metrics imply. The genuine opportunity is that this paper and Simone et al. answer complementary halves of our brief, one giving density and reconstruction, the other giving detection reliability and a topological shortcut, and neither has been applied to a real sanitary network at SA Water's scale. Running both on the same network and comparing would be a legitimate contribution rather than a replication. The available code makes the DSS side realistic within our timeline, which is the strongest practical argument for starting there.

36.citation: Zheng, Y., Jin, X., Wei, J., Zhou, Y., & Zhang, Y. (2025). A novel framework for optimization and evaluation of sensors network in urban drainage system. Water Research, 270, 122833. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2024.122833
36.intro: Urban drainage systems need sensor networks to track how they are operating and to support early flood warnings, but budget and maintenance limits mean sensors cannot be installed at every node. Most earlier work has concentrated on finding the best places to put sensors, with far less attention given to checking how well a chosen network actually performs once it is in place. This paper fills that gap by pairing placement optimisation with a separate evaluation step.
36.methods: The aim is a framework that both optimises sensor placement for flood-risk monitoring and then quantifies how well the resulting network performs. The method has three steps. First, a SWMM hydraulic model of the study catchment is run across 144 rainfall events (varying return period, duration and peak position) and 300 randomised parameter sets generated by Monte Carlo sampling, producing 43,200 simulated flood scenarios. Second, information-theory measures drive the optimisation: Value of Information, a cost-based measure of how useful a sensor reading would be, and transinformation, a measure of redundancy between nodes. These are combined in a multi-objective NSGA-II algorithm that maximises VOI while minimising both redundancy and the number of sensors. Third, matrix completion by non-negative matrix factorisation reconstructs water levels at unmonitored nodes from the readings of the chosen sensors, and the accuracy of that reconstruction is used to score the layout.
36.scope: A single catchment in HZ city, China (878 nodes, 898 conduits, 2.679 km squared) that already has three water-level sensors. Water level is the only monitored variable. Evaluation is limited to two scenarios: a non-flooding rainfall event and a serious flooding event.
36.usefulness: The paper supplies a complete, reproducible pipeline (hydraulic modelling, information-theory optimisation, matrix-completion evaluation) that could be adapted for an Adelaide catchment provided a calibrated hydraulic model is available. Plotting performance against sensor count and identifying where returns start to flatten gives a clear, quantitative way to justify a particular number of sensors to a utility such as SA Water. The finding that sensor value depends more on flooding probability than on physical distance is also a useful design principle.
36.limitations: Only water level is used as the monitored variable, the work is tested on a single catchment, and the matrix-completion step incorporates no prior topological information, which the authors themselves note could improve results if added.
36.conclusions: An optimised layout chosen with VOI and redundancy outperformed both the existing three-sensor setup and random layouts of the same size. Performance rose sharply up to roughly four to eight sensors and then levelled off, giving a practical basis for choosing between lower- and higher-budget options. Matrix completion proved an effective, low-cost way to evaluate network performance without running further hydraulic simulations.
36.reflection: Of the three papers reviewed here, this one gives the clearest working example of turning sensor placement into a decision that can be justified with numbers rather than judgement alone. For Adelaide's drainage system it suggests that, if a hydraulic model can be built or already exists, the same VOI-plus-redundancy-plus-matrix-completion pipeline could be used to test candidate sensor counts and layouts before money is spent, and to present SA Water with evidence for why a particular number of sensors was selected.

37.citation: Simone, A., Cesaro, A., Del Giudice, G., Di Cristo, C., Esposito, G., & Fecarotta, O. (2022). The spread of contaminants in urban drainage networks based on a topological analysis. Environmental Sciences Proceedings, 21(1), 20. https://doi.org/10.3390/environsciproc2022021020
37.intro: Studying how contaminants move through urban drainage networks usually means building detailed hydraulic and water-quality models, which demand a lot of data and computing power, especially on large networks. This short conference paper offers a simpler alternative that relies only on network topology and skips hydraulic simulation altogether.
37.methods: The aim is to model contaminant diffusion using topology alone and to introduce a simple index showing how easily a spill at any given node would be detected at the outfall. The network is treated as a directed graph, with contaminant travelling in the flow direction and decaying with distance. Instead of real flow rates the method uses Horton stream order, a purely topological ranking of pipe size or importance, as a stand-in for flow. Rules are set out for how concentration changes along ordinary pipes and at junctions, where dilution is a Horton-order-weighted average of the incoming pipes. A new metric, the contamination index (I_C), is defined for each node as the amount of contaminant that would reach the outfall from a spill at that node, adjusted by a length-based decay term.
37.scope: Demonstrated on a small standard test network (SWMM Example 3: 32 nodes, 32 pipes, one outfall). It is not applied to a real or large network in this paper.
37.usefulness: Of the three papers reviewed here, this one needs the least data and the lowest computational effort. Only a network map, flow directions and pipe lengths are required, with no historical records or calibrated hydraulic model. It could serve as a quick first pass over an Adelaide network, highlighting nodes from which contamination would be easy or hard to detect, before any more data-intensive work is started.
37.limitations: The approach was tested only on a small demonstration network, so its performance on a real, complex system remains unknown. The dilution and decay rules are a coarse topological approximation of actual hydraulic behaviour, and the paper does not quantify how much accuracy is lost relative to full hydraulic simulation.
37.conclusions: On the test network, contaminant concentration and detectability as measured by the contamination index followed clear and expected patterns: highest near the outfall and along major pipes, lowest on minor upstream branches. The method eliminates the need for hydraulic simulation and avoids any optimisation problem, making it cheap to apply. The authors note that testing on a real, complex network is still required.
37.reflection: This paper is most useful as a low-cost screening step rather than a finished design tool. For Adelaide it suggests a practical first move: use existing GIS pipe data to rank nodes by contamination index before any hydraulic modelling begins. That ranking could then guide where more detailed, data-heavy methods such as Zheng et al. should be applied first.

38.citation: Li, C., Singh, V. P., & Mishra, A. K. (2012). Entropy theory based criterion for hydrometric network evaluation and design: Maximum information minimum redundancy. Water Resources Research, 48(5), W05521. https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR011251
38.intro: Hydrometric monitoring networks for streamflow, water level and similar variables must be designed so that a limited number of stations collect as much useful information as possible. Earlier entropy-based design methods usually captured only one or two network properties, such as information content or redundancy, and some assumed normally distributed data, which is often unrealistic for hydrological records. This paper puts forward a more complete criterion that addresses several properties at once and does not rely on any particular data distribution.
38.methods: The aim is a criterion, and a practical way to apply it, for designing or evaluating hydrometric networks so the chosen stations carry the most information with the least duplication. The paper defines the Maximum Information Minimum Redundancy (MIMR) criterion, combining three measures: joint entropy for overall information, transinformation for how well information can be inferred from monitored to unmonitored stations, and total correlation for redundancy among the selected stations. These are combined into a single objective using adjustable weights. Continuous data are discretised with a floor function and a greedy algorithm selects stations step by step. The method is tested on two case studies: streamflow gauges on the Brazos River in Texas and a dense water-level monitoring network in a polder system in the Netherlands.
38.scope: General hydrometric network design and evaluation rather than urban drainage specifically. Both case studies involve choosing a subset of stations from an already existing, relatively dense set of candidate stations.
38.usefulness: This paper supplies the theoretical foundation for the information-theory sensor-placement methods used in the review paper and in Zheng et al. (2025). It is valuable for understanding the core logic of maximising information, maximising transferability and minimising redundancy that later urban-drainage methods build upon. The distinction it draws between information-scattered networks, where stations mostly hold unique information, and information-clustered networks, where nearby stations largely duplicate each other, offers a useful diagnostic for checking whether a proposed Adelaide sensor layout is likely to suffer from redundancy problems.
38.limitations: The method can only select a subset of stations from an already dense candidate network; it does not indicate how to expand into new, previously uninstrumented areas. It has no built-in way to account for the economic cost of adding stations, and the greedy selection algorithm is more computationally demanding than some simpler alternatives.
38.conclusions: In both case studies, MIMR selected stations that were more evenly spread and less redundant than those chosen by a comparison entropy-based method, while capturing a similar or only slightly lower share of total information. Selecting stations by variance or information content alone, without accounting for redundancy, proved insufficient, because nearby stations can appear individually informative while largely duplicating each other's data.
38.reflection: This paper clarifies the reasoning behind the information-theory methods referenced throughout the other papers reviewed. Its main practical lesson for the Adelaide work is that a good monitoring network must be checked for redundancy, not only for information content, and that this requires a sufficiently dense set of candidate points with historical or simulated data before an entropy-based selection method of this kind can be applied.

39.citation: Ninh, T.H.D., Zeng, W., Lambert, M.F., Do, N.C. & Yin, C. 2026, ‘Proactive blockage detection in sewer pipes using paired acoustic sensors: An experimental study’, Applied Acoustics, vol. 246, article 111244.
39.intro: This paper investigates the use of paired acoustic sensors, combined with a paired impulse response function technique, to detect, locate and estimate the size of blockages in sewer pipes. Unlike single-trace acoustic methods, a blockage appears in the paired impulse response as a pair of opposite-sign spikes, which makes it easier to distinguish from other features of the pipe.
39.methods: Laboratory experiments were conducted on PVC pipes under gravity flow with complex environmental noise. Blockages of low, medium and large severity were introduced, including cases representing tree root intrusion and solid material. A broadband acoustic signal was injected and the responses measured by two closely spaced sensors were used to extract the paired impulse response function. Power spectral density and coherence analysis in the frequency domain supported the interpretation. Performance was assessed on robustness, meaning how consistently blockages are detected and located, and on sensitivity, meaning how well clean and blocked conditions are separated and blockage size estimated from spike magnitude.
39.scope: Laboratory-scale testing on PVC pipe under gravity flow, covering detection, localisation and size estimation of blockages. The study addresses the measurement technique rather than sensor placement, and does not include a field deployment on an operational network.
39.usefulness: The paper states two limitations of water-level sensing that are directly relevant to placement work on gravity sewers. Level sensors may have difficulty detecting blockages at an early stage, particularly in steep sewer systems where sensor coverage is limited, and an abnormal water level recorded at a maintenance hole is insufficient to pinpoint the blockage location accurately. The first supports treating terrain as a constraint on what level-based monitoring can achieve; the second supports treating sensors as a configuration rather than as isolated points. The paper also reports local context for the problem: over 3,500 blockages from non-flushable items in the metropolitan Adelaide sewer network during 2022 to 2023, and more than two million dollars spent in 2024 removing such material from the system.
39.limitations: Testing was confined to laboratory conditions on PVC pipe, so transferability to an operational network of mixed age, material and condition is untested. The paper notes that most acoustic detection methods perform well only in controlled environments with minimal lateral connections and background noise, which is not representative of a reticulation network. The technique requires active signal injection and a pair of sensors at each measurement location, so cost and installation effort per site are higher than for passive single-point monitoring.
39.conclusions: The presence of paired spikes in the paired impulse response trace was clear evidence of a blockage, including blockages caused by tree roots and solid material. The technique identified both the location and the size of blockages with strong agreement against the conditions observed during the experiments. The authors conclude that the acoustic paired impulse response approach is a reliable method for blockage detection in sewer systems and allows utilities to act before an overflow causes environmental or public health impacts.
39.reflection: This is a detection method rather than a placement method, so it does not change how sensor locations are selected. Its value is as independent support, from the same research group that produced the topology and elevation placement method, for two claims about the limits of level sensing: that performance degrades in steep networks, and that a single instrumented chamber cannot localise a blockage within a reach. It also indicates the direction the field is moving, from detecting that something is wrong towards identifying where, which is worth considering when recommending a monitoring strategy over a multi-year horizon.

40.citation: Cheng, C., Tran, V. N., Dong, J., Whitaker, S., Bergt, S., Ziker, J., Ivanov, V. Y., & Huan, X. (2026). Matching urban flood sensor placement to monitoring objectives using Bayesian optimal experimental design (arXiv:2608.21182 [stat.AP]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.21182
40.intro: Flood-monitoring sensors are normally placed according to coverage, access, or expected inundation, but the authors argue the value of a measurement depends on the prediction or decision it is intended to inform. Flood-risk management uses inundation models to predict water depth, flow pathways and flood timing, and those predictions carry uncertainty because precipitation forcing, topography, initial conditions, model parameters and model structure are not perfectly known. Those uncertainties propagate through nonlinear flood dynamics and interact in especially complex ways in urban environments, where buildings obstruct overland flow, roadways convey runoff, and drainage systems transmit flood effects beyond the areas actually receiving rainfall. The central claim is stated plainly: flood-monitoring design must define its learning target before deciding what, where and when to measure, because a design is optimal only relative to the monitoring objective it encodes.
40.methods: Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) makes the learning target explicit by assigning each candidate location an expected utility over prospective observations. When the utility is the Kullback–Leibler divergence from the posterior to the prior, the resulting expected information gain (EIG) measures how strongly a prospective observation is expected to change the distribution of the learning target; equivalently it is the mutual information between the observation and that target. Covariance-based A-optimality (minimising the posterior covariance trace) and D-optimality (minimising its log determinant) are noted as simpler alternatives to the full-distribution criterion. Two variants are compared: parameter-oriented OED (PO-OED), which values EIG about the model parameter vector, and goal-oriented OED (GO-OED), which values EIG about a specified flood prediction Z obtained by pushing the prior and posterior parameter distributions through a fixed map H. Flood physics come from tRIBS-Urban, which represents distributed hydrologic processes and two-dimensional overland flow across the urban terrain. Because the design calculations require many flood-model evaluations across parameter realisations and candidate locations, direct use of tRIBS-Urban is computationally prohibitive, so a deep neural-network surrogate is substituted. Global sensitivity analysis (Sobol' indices) accompanies the EIG calculations. Prediction targets include three point depths one hour after observation, their joint vector, regional-average depths, and vectors of regional maximum depth at three lead times; averaging coefficients are either equal per mesh node or proportional to nodal control area, and are held distinct from the stakeholder-priority weights introduced later. Public geospatial data supply illustrative feasibility and contextual classifications for deployment screening.
40.scope: A single-sensor design problem over 2,576 candidate locations for the August 2014 storm in the I-696–Mound Road corridor of metropolitan Detroit, with a six-parameter uncertainty model and one historical precipitation forcing. The domain is urban pluvial flooding rather than in-pipe sewer monitoring, though the drainage network is part of the modelled system. Out of scope: multi-sensor networks, adaptive or mobile sampling schedules, uncertain future rainfall, additional flood events, and any cost model for installation or operation.
40.usefulness: This is the clearest statement I have read of the argument that the objective has to be fixed before the placement problem is even well posed, and it is directly transferable to our project: 'optimal' sensor locations for blockage detection, overflow prevention and flow reconstruction are not the same locations, and the paper gives a formal reason why. The EIG-as-mutual-information equivalence is the same quantity Crowley et al. (2025) maximise for sewer networks — that paper is cited here as reference [8] — so the two sit on a common footing and can be presented together in our review rather than as separate methods. Two other pieces are worth taking. First, the surrogate pattern: an expensive physical model is run once to train a neural-network emulator, and the design search then runs against the emulator, which is exactly how we would make repeated SWMM-based evaluation tractable. Second, the explicit separation of information value from deployability — the paper's point that an informative sensor location is not automatically deployable because access, safety, power, communications, permission, maintenance and organisational responsibility all restrict placement — is the constraint layer SA Water will care about, and this paper shows a defensible way to fold it in as a feasibility screen rather than an afterthought.
40.limitations: The authors are candid about the controlled nature of the setting: one urban domain, one historical precipitation forcing and a single-sensor design problem, chosen deliberately to isolate how the monitoring objective changes placement, but therefore not an operational forecasting study. The six-parameter model and the neural-network surrogate likewise provide a focused rather than realistic uncertainty description; the authors note that future work should test sensitivity to the prior and to the observation-error model, expand the uncertain inputs to precipitation, topography, boundary conditions, spatial parameter variation, observation-model misspecification and model discrepancy, and validate the surrogate across the prior, wet and dry regimes and at high-EIG locations to establish whether it preserves the spatial rankings. They also flag that repeated nested Monte Carlo calculations would be needed to distinguish close competitors, particularly for the weighted multi-point cases. Beyond what they state: the point locations and target regions were chosen to isolate the effect of the learning target rather than drawn from a real warning threshold, asset or response decision, so the reported rankings are illustrative; the feasibility classification is built from public geospatial data and is explicitly not field-verified; and the data are available only from the corresponding author on request, so nothing here is independently reproducible.
40.conclusions: Three conclusions are drawn. First, parameter EIG and prediction EIG support different monitoring purposes: the estimated Sobol' indices indicate interaction effects among the uncertain parameters, and the PO-OED example shows that learning the full parameter vector transfers unevenly into reductions in predictive uncertainty across locations and lead times. Second, the prediction target shapes the spatial ranking — point-depth targets favour nearby locations, whereas regional-average and regional-maximum-depth targets can favour nonlocal locations, and weighted multi-point objectives preserve similar broad spatial patterns while their computed max-EIG locations fall in one of two visually competitive regions. Third, information value and deployability belong in the same design process but require different evidence: public geospatial classifications can organise initial screening, while verified field conditions determine which informative locations are actually feasible to install and operate. The recommended practice is an objective-first workflow — define the intended prediction and priority weights, use field-verified restrictions to set the admissible set, compute the information map, identify high-EIG locations, then interpret them with hydraulic and graded feasibility evidence.
40.reflection: The most useful thing this paper does for our team is give us language for a problem we keep tripping over: when the client asks where to put sensors, the honest first response is a question about what they want to learn. Framing our deliverable as objective-first rather than algorithm-first would make the report stronger and is cheap to adopt. The caution is that this is a flood-inundation study on an overland domain, not a sewer study, and I would not present its numerical results as sewer evidence — its value to us is methodological. It is also worth noting how much machinery is required for a single sensor: a distributed hydrologic model, a trained surrogate, nested Monte Carlo EIG estimation and a global sensitivity analysis, all to rank 2,576 candidates for one device. If we want anything comparable for a network of sensors across an Adelaide catchment, the greedy or submodular route used in the sewer literature is the realistic path, and this paper is best cited as the theoretical justification for what that greedy objective should be measuring.

41.citation: Drenoyanis, A., & Prackwieser, C. (2022, May 11). Detecting wastewater blockages with digital water meters? A survey of methods used by Sydney Water. Water e-Journal, Australian Water Association. https://info.awa.asn.au/water-e-journal/detecting-wastewater-blockages-with-digital-water-meters-a-survey-of-methods-used-by-sydney-water
41.intro: Dry-weather wastewater overflows and their impact on customers and the environment are described as a challenge for utilities across Australia. The majority of blockages in the wastewater network are caused by tree roots penetrating pipes and access chambers, wet wipes, fat/oil/grease, or a combination of those, and most occur in small-diameter pipes — the so-called wastewater reticulation network. Sydney Water's IoT programme has already deployed thousands of blockage-detection devices; this paper surveys the methods the utility uses and trials, and proposes incorporating water-usage data from upstream digital meters to improve the diurnal prediction models that raise blockage alerts.
41.methods: The paper is a practitioner survey rather than a controlled study. It sets out the countermeasures available (regular manual access-chamber and CCTV pipe inspections, monitoring technologies combined with analytics, cyclic cleaning and root-cutting, follow-on repairs and rehabilitation, continuous lining, and customer campaigns), and the three device types tested and deployed: level switches/float sensors that alarm at a pre-defined level; ultrasonic/radar level sensors that measure sewer height to centimetre accuracy every 15 minutes and submit readings daily or on alarm; and sewer flow sensors that measure volume through a pipe. Device selection is governed by a technical specification covering communication network, protocols and security, plus a corrosive-environment casing with no aluminium or steel, IP68 rating for high humidity and occasional immersion, vermin- and cockroach-resistant cables and seals, safe mounting brackets, external antennas at roughly 90% of sites because devices sit in concrete pits under metal lids, and long battery life to avoid re-visits; NB-IoT is the preferred protocol for this metropolitan use case over LoRaWAN. Site selection follows a ten-step process: prioritise a sub-catchment by number of dry-weather overflows and licence limits; inspect the asset on site including signal testing; carry out repairs and root-cutting; assign each asset a risk rating combining likelihood of blocking or choking with environmental consequence of failure (incorporating sewer location and pipe size); generate a risk rating for pipeline chains by calculating probability of failure of assets connected in series; produce an asset priority list; have subject-matter experts assess sites spatially and decide on location parameters; assess safety and accessibility; run environmental, heritage and traffic-control assessments where required; and refine the delivery plan. Three analytics methods are described: pumping-station inflow comparison against historical diurnal patterns, a paired upstream/downstream comparison between IoT chambers, and correlation of digital water-meter consumption against derived sewer flow.
41.scope: Operational dry-weather blockage and overflow detection in Sydney Water's reticulation network, at utility scale. Includes device selection, site prioritisation, alarm analytics and a digital-water-meter trial in the Liverpool area, plus an early-stage trial monitoring receiving waterways such as creeks and stormwater channels. Out of scope: any formal placement optimisation, hydraulic modelling, wet-weather overflow, and quantitative model validation.
41.usefulness: This is the most practically grounded item in my set and the only one that tells us what a large Australian utility actually does, which makes it directly comparable to SA Water. Three things are worth carrying into our report. First, the risk-based site-selection process is a real, working alternative to mathematical optimisation, and the step that calculates probability of failure for pipeline chains connected in series is close to a coverage argument in disguise — it is the sort of thing our optimisation could formalise rather than replace. Second, the paper quantifies the value case: the solution detects on average 20 blockages per month, more than 300 blockages at environmentally high-risk sites have been identified and cleared, and this represents approximately $400,000 in avoided incident costs per month, though the authors say this is far outweighed by non-financial benefits including protection of the environment, community amenity, public health and employee safety. That is exactly the kind of number a client-facing report needs. Third, the hardware specification list is a ready-made constraints checklist for our candidate-node feasibility layer: corrosive-resistant casing, IP68, vermin-resistant cabling, external antennas at ~90% of sites, and battery life as a first-order design driver.
41.limitations: The authors are unusually explicit about where their methods fail. The pumping-station method can detect overflows and some blockages anywhere upstream of a sewer pumping station by comparing wet-well inflow rates and pump runtimes against historical diurnal patterns, but it relies on the lost flow being statistically significant compared with normal total inflow, so chokes that are a small proportion of typical station flow cannot be distinguished from natural variation; and it localises the fault only to potentially tens of kilometres of network. The paired upstream/downstream method is limited by telemetry rather than physics: devices are configured to measure level every 15 minutes and submit all readings once a day to preserve battery, so backend comparison of two sites can only happen retrospectively for the last 24 hours, and a real-time alarm based on the difference between two IoT sites is currently not possible; call-in frequency can be increased but at the expense of battery consumption. Where inflows from properties or other sewers enter between the two devices, those inflows have to be predicted from historical flow data. The digital-meter correlation degrades in rain — 0.97 on a dry day against 0.79 on a rainy day — and water used for irrigation and pool top-ups may never enter the sewer at all. The waterway-monitoring trial is judged to need significant maintenance effort and anomaly-detection algorithms most likely fine-tuned per install site, so in its current design it suits only some sites. Beyond what is stated: this is a non-peer-reviewed industry paper with no DOI, no reported detection rate against a ground-truth set of blockages, and no false-alarm statistics.
41.conclusions: Level sensors are preferred over float switches because they provide much more detailed data useful for prediction and modelling and tell operations teams how fast the wastewater level is rising, which — combined with historical flow data at the site and time-of-day — is used to estimate required response times; at the time of writing they are deployed at sites with very high consequence of failure or very shallow access chambers. Instrumenting reticulation access chambers significantly reduces the search area compared with pumping-station alarms alone, and allows a two-sided diagnosis: a sustained normalised positive flow error (level or derived flow above expected) suggests a choke or partial choke downstream of the chamber, while a sustained normalised negative flow error suggests one upstream. Many of the chokes identified so far have been in bushland where overflows are not in public view and could have run for days before being reported. The digital-water-meter work remains a trial; the backend compares upstream and downstream measurements and alarms on significant deviation from prediction.
41.reflection: This paper is the reality check for the optimisation literature I have been reading. Every mathematically elegant placement method I have looked at assumes any node can host a sensor and that data arrive continuously; Sydney Water's experience says roughly 90% of sites need an external antenna, devices report once a day to protect battery, and a real-time cross-site comparison is not currently possible. If those constraints hold at SA Water too, then a placement solution that depends on synchronised high-frequency readings from adjacent chambers is not deployable as designed, and we should say so explicitly rather than discovering it at the end. The other thing I keep returning to is the bushland finding — blockages running for days because nobody could see them. That is a consequence-of-failure argument for putting sensors where nobody is watching rather than where the most people are, which is the opposite of what a pure coverage objective would give you, and it is worth raising with the client early.

42.citation: Li, N., Wang, X., Li, Z., Zhao, F., Nair, A., Zhang, J., & Liu, C. (2023). Real-time identification and positioning of sewer blockage based on liquid level analysis in rural area. Processes, 11(1), 161. https://doi.org/10.3390/pr11010161
42.intro: Sewage from urban areas is collected by sewer and transported to a treatment plant, but sediment, domestic garbage, crop straw and similar substances deposit easily where there is insufficient flow power, clogging the sewer. Rural Chinese networks are particularly exposed: small diameters (DN100–DN300) and inferior operation and maintenance management limit stable operation, and blockage is related to pipe diameter, slope and pipeline ageing. Efficient and accurate identification and positioning of blockage reduces the need for earthwork excavation and supports environmental protection and waterlogging mitigation. The authors' premise is that after a blockage the sewage is intercepted and the liquid level changes upstream and downstream of the blocking point, so monitoring level on both sides can identify and locate the obstruction.
42.methods: The paper reviews existing detection technology first — video, sonar, radar and ultrasonic sensing via in-pipe robots, CCTV and laser detection, and machine-learning approaches including qualitative trend analysis, random forest and support vector machines — and notes that acoustic detection is simple and low-cost but limited by fault-extraction methods and low discrimination between fault features, while in-pipe robots still struggle with the complexity of drainage pipelines. The proposed method instead uses a network of liquid-level sensors, feasible because IoT makes real-time mass monitoring possible; the level sensors have 1 mm accuracy, so multiple units are needed to form a monitoring network. Two experiment scales were run. The pilot-scale rig used PVC pipe with flow driven by a pump into a storage tank and regulated by an outlet valve, level sensors upstream and downstream of the blocking point, a 15 s sampling interval and 13 min per experimental group; flow was varied from 0.5 to 5 m³/h, selected from a daily consumption of 40 L per inhabitant to represent a population range of 130–1,300 people. The full-scale experiment installed six liquid-level sensors at manhole wellheads. A double-threshold discriminant rule was then built: if the level change rate exceeds a positive threshold a and the level change range exceeds A simultaneously, a blockage downstream of that gauge is declared; if the change rate falls below a negative threshold b and the change range falls below B simultaneously, a blockage upstream is declared; otherwise operation is normal. Threshold values were derived from the pilot- and full-scale experiments, producing a blockage identification and positioning matrix.
42.scope: Gravity sanitary sewers in rural areas, DN150 to DN300, under both low and peak water-consumption periods, with blockages introduced at known manholes and blocking objects of 0.1, 0.15 and 0.2 kg dry weight. The method addresses detection and relative positioning of a blockage against the sensor layout; it does not attempt to optimise sensor placement, model hydraulics, or classify blockage type.
42.usefulness: The result our project can use most directly is the spacing guidance. The authors find that although level change can still be monitored a long distance downstream after an upstream blockage — a sensor detected change 180 m upstream of itself — it is advisable not to exceed 100 m between monitoring points if identification performance is to hold. That is a concrete, empirically grounded upper bound on sensor spacing for small-diameter gravity sewers, and it is the sort of number that turns an abstract coverage constraint into something a utility can cost. The paper also supplies detection-rate evidence by distance and blockage severity, and the double-threshold discriminant is simple enough to reimplement without a hydraulic model, which makes it a plausible baseline against which to compare anything more sophisticated we build. The framing that blockage produces a rise upstream and a drop downstream, with the sensor's position relative to the blockage recoverable from which of the two signatures it sees, is also the mechanism that makes paired or sequential placement meaningful rather than arbitrary.
42.limitations: Detection quality degrades sharply with distance from the blockage. Within 4 m upstream of the blocking point the identification rate was 95.3%, attributed precisely to the monitoring point being close to the blockage; when the monitoring point is far from the blockage the level rise cannot be detected in a short time. In the pilot-scale DN200 experiments 20% of blockages were misjudged as normal operation, and in the full-scale experiments 16.7% of post-blockage level drops could not be judged as blocked. The thresholds themselves are empirical, derived from these specific rigs, diameters and flow ranges, and no procedure is given for transferring them to a different network or recalibrating them in service. The pilot rig used clean pumped water rather than real wastewater, so sediment transport, fat and grease behaviour and solids accumulation are not represented; blockages were introduced artificially by dry weight rather than developing over time, which is the case a proactive system actually has to catch. Populations were inferred from an assumed 40 L per person per day. The paper reports no false-positive rate under normal operation for the pilot rig, and the full-scale claim that the sewer was never misjudged as obstructed under normal operation rests on a small number of runs.
42.conclusions: Within a minute of blocking, abnormal level rise can be monitored within 4 m upstream of the blocking point, and within 4 minutes the level reaches a peak 300% to 700% higher than before the blockage, with the increase positively related to the degree of blocking. Downstream, a significant drop in level is detectable. The identification rate downstream of the blocking point was 93.3%, and a 0.2 kg dry-weight blockage was identified 100% of the time at 29.55 m and 60.4 m downstream, while 0.15 kg and 0.1 kg blockages gave 93.3%. Overall success rates for the discriminant model, covering both normal operation and blockage, were 80.4% in the pilot-scale experiments (DN200, 80% for blockage cases) and 95.6% in the full-scale experiments (DN300, 83.3% for blockage cases). The relative position of the blockage is recovered from which sensor sees an abnormal level and in which direction it moves.
42.reflection: This is the paper I would cite when someone asks why sensor density matters rather than just sensor position. The 100 m recommendation and the drop from 95.3% detection at 4 m to substantially worse performance further away make the coverage-versus-count trade-off physical instead of notional, and they set a ceiling on how sparse an optimal layout can honestly be. The obvious caveat for our context is that this is a rural Chinese network at DN150–DN300 with an assumed 40 L per person per day; Adelaide reticulation is a different beast in flow regime and diurnal shape, so the specific thresholds will not transfer even if the mechanism does. What I would like to test, if we get real SA Water level data, is whether the same double-threshold rule fires on their historical blockage records — it is cheap to implement and would give us a defensible baseline before we claim any improvement from an optimised layout.

43.citation: Lin, R., Qiu, R., Hu, L., Ding, Y., & Yuan, Z. (2025). A low-cost soft sensor for sewer flow monitoring — Learning from water level measurements in manholes. Water Research, 274, 123135. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2025.123135
43.intro: Flow rates in sewers are usually measured at manholes with flow meters, especially ultrasonic Doppler meters, but several reasons hinder their large-scale deployment. Besides high costs, flow meters require frequent maintenance and have low durability because direct contact with wastewater or stormwater causes fouling and even failure. A water level sensor costs only a small fraction of a flow meter, is much more durable, and can work continuously for multiple years without noticeable performance degradation, whereas significant drift can be observed in flow meters even in the first month — something the authors also see in their own data. A data-driven soft sensor estimates a variable that is difficult or expensive to measure from other, more easily measured variables, so a soft flow sensor driven by water level is an attractive proposition. Level has already been used this way at combined sewer overflow structures, where earlier work fitted empirical polynomial, weir or rating-curve equations, and where CFD-calibrated soft sensors achieved errors typically within 10% and, for a real CSO in Aarhus validated against ultrasonic level sensors and an electromagnetic flow meter, under 3% for most events.
43.methods: The obstacle is that the level–flow relationship in a manhole is not a rating curve. Flows into and out of a manhole may be free-surface or pressurised, and subcritical, critical or supercritical, producing a non-bijective and even multivalued relationship in which one water depth can correspond to two or more flow rates. The authors' response is to feed the model a time series rather than a single depth: from a physical standpoint the flow rate at time i−n is influenced by water depths at earlier steps (the domain of dependence for the Navier–Stokes equations) and affects depths at later steps (the domain of influence), so both past and future depth values carry critical information about the current flow rate. The soft sensor is a multilayer perceptron whose input is a window of measured levels spanning both earlier and later measurements around the target instant, and whose output is the corresponding flow rate; one hidden layer with 128 neurons was chosen as the balance between performance, computational cost and over-fitting risk. Training data came from three manholes (M561, M536, M570) with significantly different hydraulic characteristics in three urbanised areas in China, recorded at 1-minute intervals across 2021 by a sensor measuring level by static pressure and flow by the Doppler effect, and covering free-surface, pressurised, subcritical and supercritical flows; only a small number of dry-weather events was kept in the training set, since too many repetitive dry-weather events reduce performance in wet weather, which matters more for operation and management. A fourth, simulated manhole generated by a three-dimensional CFD model was used to probe robustness, with water-level sensor error modelled as Gaussian with zero bias and a 95% confidence interval of 3 mm (μ = 0, σ = 1.5 mm) after commercial product specifications. Ablations covered input window size, sampling frequency (1 s to 2 min on the simulated manhole) and hidden-layer width.
43.scope: Flow estimation at a single instrumented manhole from that manhole's own level record, demonstrated on three real manholes and one CFD-simulated manhole. Covers dry and wet weather, free-surface and pressurised flow. Out of scope: sensor placement, network-scale flow reconstruction from sparse sensors, blockage or overflow detection, and any manhole without a prior flow-measurement campaign.
43.usefulness: This paper changes the cost model that sits underneath any placement study, which is why it matters to us. If a level sensor plus a trained MLP can stand in for a Doppler flow meter, then the budget constraint in an optimisation problem is no longer 'how many flow meters can we afford' but 'how many level sensors can we afford, plus how many temporary flow campaigns'. Given that a level sensor costs more than an order of magnitude less than a flow meter and needs annual rather than weekly maintenance, that is a large shift in achievable sensor density, and it is exactly the kind of argument SA Water would want quantified. The methodological insight worth borrowing is the use of a symmetric time window around the target instant: because the depth–flow relationship at a manhole is genuinely multivalued, a single-instant input cannot resolve it, and the paper's ablation (Fig. 6) shows the windowed variants clearly outperforming the point-in-time and linear alternatives. Finally, the reconstruction of flow for a period when the flow meter was malfunctioning is a use case in its own right — data quality assurance for an existing monitoring fleet — which may be an easier first win for a utility than a new deployment.
43.limitations: The authors are direct about the training-data problem: both water level and flow rate data are required to train the soft sensor, which could hinder widespread application because a comprehensive measurement campaign is needed for each manhole, covering dry weather and a variety of wet-weather conditions, and each campaign incurs considerable labour cost. The economics also depend on retraining frequency — if frequent retraining is needed, for example because of rapid sewer sediment buildup, the soft sensor will not be as cost-effective, and the authors suggest permanently installing a flow meter and level sensor in parallel so the frequently calibrated soft sensor can verify the flow-meter data instead. Robustness is asymmetric: the sensor is insensitive to random noise on either signal, and tolerated a fixed −30 mm level bias when trained on the biased data, but a −30 mm bias applied only at test time (9.00% mean relative error in the input) produced systematically low estimates at 11.80% MRE, and a −0.08 m³/s bias in the training flow data (26.18% MRE in the input) produced 37.62% MRE — an amplification of 34.55%. In short, the quality of the flow rate data is critical. Beyond what is stated: the models are per-manhole and no transfer to an uninstrumented manhole is attempted; the downstream condition of each manhole was unknown; and the optimal 4-minute window and 1-minute sampling are tied to these sites.
43.conclusions: The MLP produced satisfactory flow estimates in the test phase for all three real manholes and the simulated one, despite their different hydraulic characteristics, and handled the nonlinear and multivalued depth–flow relationship that defeats rating-curve approaches. The optimal input window is around 4 minutes: a 2-minute window omits key information, while windows of 12 minutes or more degrade performance because of the increased number of parameters to train. A 1-minute sampling frequency is sufficient. Robustness testing on the simulated manhole gave a baseline MRE of 2.88% and NSE of 0.9372, degrading only to 2.90%/0.9337 with Gaussian noise on depth, 3.26%/0.9223 when the 95% confidence interval was widened from 3 mm to 10 mm (larger than any product specification the authors found), 3.32%/0.9318 with noise on the flow data, and 3.38%/0.9262 with noise on both. The authors conclude the soft sensor is a potentially cheaper and more durable alternative to traditional flow meters for sewer applications, with robustness further improvable by raising the measurement frequency and adding a noise-reduction filter.
43.reflection: The finding I did not expect is that the model needs future water levels as well as past ones, and that this is not a trick but a consequence of the Navier–Stokes domain of influence. It means a soft flow sensor is inherently slightly retrospective, which is fine for hydraulic modelling and I/I accounting but is a real constraint if we wanted the same device to raise a real-time overflow alarm — worth stating plainly in our review rather than letting 'soft sensor' sound like a free substitution. For the capstone, the honest reading is that this lowers the marginal cost of a monitoring point but does not remove the need for flow data; someone still has to run a campaign at every manhole they want a soft sensor at. That makes the pairing with the follow-up Water Research X paper important, since that one is precisely about reducing the flow-data requirement, and I would present the two together rather than separately.

44.citation: Lin, R., Tian, W., Qiu, R., Hu, L., & Yuan, Z. (2025). Low-cost, data-efficient, on-device soft sensors for sewer flow monitoring — learning from adjacent water level sensors. Water Research X, 29, 100415. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wroa.2025.100415
44.intro: This is the follow-up to the same group's single-manhole soft sensor, and it targets that method's main weakness. Flow measurements are critical for sewer monitoring, but it is challenging to deploy large numbers of flow meters on large-scale networks because of their high costs and low durability. Soft sensors that derive flow from water depth are more cost-effective, but training them still requires extensive direct flow measurements — which is exactly the barrier to scale. The proposal here is to read water depth at two adjacent manholes rather than one, so that the extra hydraulic information reduces how much flow data the sensor needs to learn from, and to run the resulting model on the device itself.
44.methods: Three model structures are implemented for the same two-depth input and compared: the Saint-Venant equations (SVE) solved with an HLL Riemann solver, in which only two parameters — Manning roughness n and sediment depth ds — are calibrated; a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with 12 input neurons representing the depth measurements, one hidden layer of 128 neurons, ReLU activations, Kaiming initialisation, Adam at learning rate 1e-3, batch size 1024 and MSE loss, implemented in PyTorch; and a physics-informed neural network (PINN), which was developed in the literature to address the data inefficiency and poor interpretability of purely data-driven methods by embedding the governing physical laws, and which here adds the two-manhole depth measurements as an extra loss term. Hardware is explicit: two water level sensors, each connected to a Raspberry Pi 5, with the downstream unit transmitting depth to the upstream unit over LoRa (SX1268 433 MHz HAT); the upstream Raspberry Pi runs the soft-sensor algorithm in real time. Only the application phase runs on-device — training was done on a desktop with an i7-13700K and an Nvidia 4070. Data came from two real sewer pipes in urbanised areas of China, both instrumented at upstream and downstream manholes with THWater TWQ flow meters and TWC level sensors at 1-minute intervals: Case Study 1 is 600 mm diameter, slope 0.005, 70 m long, 38 days and 52,026 samples covering dry and wet weather, with average dry-weather inflow around 210 m³/d rising up to about five times in wet weather; Case Study 2 is 1,200 mm diameter, slope 0.005, 113 m long, two weeks and 20,075 samples, average inflow about 16,505 m³/d, dry weather only. A virtual pipe with Case Study 1's geometry was simulated across 20 scenarios varying roughness from 0.015 to 0.04 and sediment depth from 0% to 80% of pipe radius, used for both parameter recovery and error-robustness testing. Data efficiency was assessed by shrinking the Case Study 1 development set from 3 hours (180 records) to 35 days (50,400 records).
44.scope: Flow estimation for a single pipe reach between two instrumented manholes, on-device, in real time. Two real pipes plus one simulated pipe, covering dry weather in both cases and wet weather in Case Study 1. Out of scope: sensor placement, network-scale reconstruction, and pipes where only one manhole can be instrumented.
44.usefulness: The data-efficiency result is the one that matters for a placement study. If the SVE-based sensor reaches an MRE of 14.7% trained on three hours of data and 13.0% on one day — with no wet-weather flows in that one-day set at all — then the commissioning cost per monitoring point collapses from a multi-season campaign to a short visit, and the number of soft flow sensors a utility could realistically afford changes by an order of magnitude. That directly loosens the budget constraint we would write into an optimisation. The paired-manhole architecture is also interesting for its own sake: it means the natural unit of instrumentation is a pipe reach rather than a point, which is closer to how a coverage objective over links (rather than nodes) is usually formulated in the placement literature. The hardware section is unusually concrete for a Water Research paper and useful to us as an existence proof — a Raspberry Pi 5 and a LoRa link are enough to produce an estimate every 0.0007 s (MLP) or 1.5 s (SVE), both suitable for real-time use. Finally, the SVE calibration returns physically meaningful parameters: n and ds were recovered as statistically identical to the true values in all simulated scenarios, and estimated as 0.0249 ± 0.0008 with 5.2 ± 0.9 mm sediment in Case Study 1 and 0.0441 ± 0.0020 with 31.9 ± 1.2 mm in Case Study 2. A sensor that also reports accumulating sediment depth is a blockage-precursor signal, not just a flow meter substitute.
44.limitations: The PINN failed outright. Because it has no separate training step and must be trained at every time step, the 60-second sampling interval always terminated training on time rather than on the performance criterion, and the resulting estimates fitted poorly — R² of −1.334 and −0.324, MRE of 97.58% and 163.18%, RMSE of 0.56633 and 0.43528 in Cases 1 and 2. The authors conclude PINN is less efficient than classic PDE solvers for a well-posed PDE problem in both computational efficiency and convergence, cite several recent studies reporting the same, and drop it from further investigation. The two remaining sensors trade off against each other rather than dominating: the MLP is more accurate when data are plentiful (MRE 5.09% vs 11.8% at 35 days) but needs 54.7% MRE at three hours and only reaches 5.60% at 11 days, with each of the two rain events in that window producing a sharp improvement — so the MLP does need wet-weather flows in training, a common shortcoming of data-driven models. The SVE sensor is rigid, with only two learned parameters, and has prediction errors wherever the real hydraulics are not fully described by the Saint-Venant equations, which is why its simulated-case performance (<0.01% MRE) is far better than its real-pipe performance. SVE training is also much slower (16.4 h vs 15.5 min) because gradients are estimated numerically rather than by automatic differentiation. Beyond what is stated: Case Study 2 has no wet-weather data at all, so the data-efficiency analysis rests on a single pipe; both pipes are short (70 m and 113 m) and both are instrumented at both ends with existing flow meters, which is precisely the situation the method is meant to avoid needing; and in Case Study 1 the downstream flows were dominated by external inflows, which the method does not explicitly account for.
44.conclusions: Both the SVE- and MLP-based soft sensors reliably estimate flow rates with a computational load light enough for a Raspberry Pi 5. On the real pipes the MLP was the more accurate of the two — R² 0.945 vs 0.931 in Case Study 1 and 0.914 vs 0.754 in Case Study 2, with the gap widest during wet-weather events and at lower flows. Across the 20 simulated roughness and sediment scenarios the SVE sensor was near-exact (MRE below 0.01% in the tested cases) while the MLP stayed below 3% MRE in all cases, confirming its strong ability to learn from data. Both were insensitive to random measurement noise; with a +5 mm bias on the upstream level sensor (12.8% of mean water depth) the MLP achieved 0.54% MRE against the SVE's 7.92%, because the MLP could learn from the biased data. The overall recommendation is that the SVE-based sensor is preferable when flow data are scarce and the MLP when they are abundant, and the authors suggest a hybrid in which SVE captures the fundamental dynamics and a data-driven model learns the residual, or an augmented Saint-Venant formulation with additional components to absorb the discrepancy.
44.reflection: Read alongside the single-manhole paper, this pair tells a coherent story that I think belongs in our review as one entry rather than two: cheap level sensors can substitute for flow meters, and the remaining obstacle — needing flow data to train each one — is substantially solved by embedding hydraulics instead of learning everything from scratch. The negative PINN result is worth reporting honestly, because physics-informed networks are fashionable and a client or supervisor may well ask why we are not using one; having a published, quantified failure on exactly this problem is a better answer than an opinion. The caveat I keep coming back to is that both real pipes already had flow meters at both ends, so the paper demonstrates that less flow data is needed, not that none is. For SA Water, the practical question is whether they have any reaches with paired instrumentation we could use to reproduce this, and that is worth asking at the same time as the CCTV question.

45.citation: Wang, Y., Huang, B., & Zhu, D. Z. (2024). Assessment of rainfall-derived inflow and infiltration in sewer systems with machine learning approaches. Water Science & Technology, 89(8), 1928–1943. https://doi.org/10.2166/wst.2024.115
45.intro: Inflow and infiltration into defective sewers increases sewage volumes and reduces treatment efficiency at wastewater treatment plants. During heavy rainfall, systems can become overloaded by rainfall-derived inflow and infiltration (RDII) and release untreated sewage and other pollutants into the environment, damaging ecosystems and posing a health risk to nearby residents. The authors' target is the weakness of the traditional RDII toolkit. The methods commonly used in the literature — the constant unit rate method, the percentage of rainfall volume (R-value) method, the percentage of stream flow method, the synthetic unit hydrograph method, the probabilistic method, rainfall/sewer flow regression, synthetic stream flow regression, and methods embedded in hydraulic software — are all constrained in ways that matter operationally. The R-value method can be used when monitoring data are lacking but its accuracy is restricted by inconsistent judgement between analysts, and the rainfall/flow regression method typically applies multiple linear regression, which is so sensitive to frequently occurring values that they distort the coefficients and interfere with predictions; its accuracy is high only when application storms resemble the storms the equations were fitted to, and the choice of those storms is subject to human subjective influence.
45.methods: Two machine learning algorithms — random forest (RF) and long short-term memory (LSTM) — were developed for sewer flow prediction, with RDII then derived from the predicted flows. Two sites in Ningbo City, China were used: the Bailong residential area in Zhenhai District, a combined sewer system, and the Wantou area in Jiangbei District, a separate sewer system. Flow and rainfall came from online monitoring systems at both sites, with THWater TWQ Series flow meters distributed across manholes and initially calibrated against HACH FL900AV meters, and rainfall recorded by a THWater THR Series tipping-bucket rain gauge with 0.2 mm accuracy. Data were collected at 1-minute frequency and resampled to 5 minutes for modelling. Feature engineering extracted physically significant features for sewer flow modelling, and a sequential forward feature selection method identified the most pertinent features from the full dataset, with rainfall retained as the external feature because of its strong effect on flow during and after events. Dry weather flow (DWF) at each time of day was computed by averaging all dry days in the same month, and RDII taken as the difference between DWF and observed wet weather flow. ARIMA was considered and rejected: as an autoregressive model it needs a stationary series, struggles with the nonlinear patterns prevalent in this dataset, and loses effectiveness on large datasets with diverse input features. Model accuracy was additionally tested by resampling at 5, 10, 20, 30 and 60 minutes.
45.scope: RDII quantification from field flow and rainfall monitoring in one combined and one separate sewer catchment, validated over eight typical rainfall events across the two sites with depths ranging from about 9.5 mm to 78.5 mm. Out of scope: sensor placement, spatial attribution of I/I sources within a catchment, and any structural inspection of the pipes whose defects are inferred.
45.usefulness: The finding our project can act on is the monitoring-frequency result, because it is a direct statement about what a sensor has to do rather than about where it goes. Accuracy was highest at 5 minutes and degraded monotonically as the interval lengthened; going from 5 to 60 minutes cost R² 0.154 (RF) and 0.222 (LSTM) at Bailong and 0.208 (RF) and 0.225 (LSTM) at Wantou, with LSTM losing more than RF because a sequence model has more to lose when information is thinned. Set against the Sydney Water paper's account of devices reporting every 15 minutes and calling in once a day to preserve battery, this is a concrete tension we can put in front of a client: the telemetry cadence that makes a battery last also degrades the analytics it feeds. The paper also gives a clean contrast between system types that is useful when reasoning about where monitoring pays off — combined systems show more flow fluctuation because stormwater and sanitary sewage share pipes, producing complex, highly autocorrelated patterns, while separate systems isolate household wastewater, giving a more dependable, weather-resistant and therefore less autocorrelated sanitary flow. Finally, the recovery-time signature is a diagnostic in its own right: Bailong's flow returned quickly to DWF after rain, while Wantou took two to three days, which the authors read as evidence of mixed connections or structural defects in a system that by design should not be receiving stormwater.
45.limitations: The RDII target is itself derived, not measured: it is the difference between observed wet weather flow and a monthly-average DWF pattern, so it can come out negative for small rainfall amounts when calculated DWF exceeds observed DWF. The authors attribute the scatter around the rainfall–RDII trendline at Wantou to exactly this — the selected DWF pattern not aligning with the actual DWF on the day of the event, since Wantou's DWF did not consistently follow a similar pattern. Model quality therefore inherits the quality of an assumption rather than a measurement. The authors also note that machine learning performance depends on the algorithms' ability to convert datasets into regression models, and that models are much easier to train and estimate accurately when the dataset has strong regularity — a candid admission that these results may not transfer to a messier catchment. Higher monitoring frequency increases available information but also increases running time. Beyond what is stated: two catchments in one city is a thin basis for a general claim; no uncertainty bounds are reported on the RDII volumes; the comparison against traditional methods is against a single published R-value result rather than a re-implementation on the same data; and the models are catchment-specific with no test of transfer to an unmonitored catchment, which is where RDII estimation is hardest.
45.conclusions: Both models achieved high accuracy in sewer flow prediction and the LSTM outperformed the RF, which the authors attribute to LSTM's capacity for long-term dependencies and nonlinear relationships in time series and its ability to process whole sequences. The LSTM predicted the temporal pattern of RDII with satisfactory accuracy across a wide range of rainfall events, and maximum relative errors on estimated RDII volume were under 7%, which the authors present as more accurate than the R-value method used in earlier work on the same kind of problem. Rainfall showed a good linear relationship with RDII in both simulated and observed results at Bailong, consistent with rainfall directly driving infiltration and inflow. Machine learning models simulated the temporal variation of the RDII process and improved prediction accuracy for peak flows and RDII volumes during storm events, compared with traditional methods that mainly produce lumped volumes.
45.reflection: This paper is not about sensor placement, and I would be careful not to overclaim it in the review — but it answers a question that placement work usually skips, which is what sampling rate the chosen sensors need to run at for the downstream analytics to work. Pairing its 5-minute result with Sydney Water's battery-driven 15-minute-and-daily-upload reality gives us a genuinely useful design constraint to raise with SA Water, and it is the sort of practical detail a client notices. The other thing worth carrying forward is the Wantou result: a separate system taking two to three days to return to dry weather flow is a strong, cheap indicator of defective pipes, derived purely from existing flow monitoring. If SA Water has separate sewers with long recovery tails, that is a way to prioritise where condition assessment and monitoring should go without needing any new instrumentation first.

46.citation: Zhang, Z., Laakso, T., Wang, Z., Pulkkinen, S., Ahopelto, S., Virrantaus, K., Li, Y., Cai, X., Zhang, C., Vahala, R., & Sheng, Z. (2020). Comparative study of AI-based methods — Application of analyzing inflow and infiltration in sanitary sewer subcatchments. Sustainability, 12(15), 6254. https://doi.org/10.3390/su12156254
46.intro: Inflow and infiltration (I/I) is a common problem in sanitary sewer systems, and the I/I rate is also treated as an important indicator of the operational and structural condition of the system. Situation awareness in sanitary sewers requires accurate wastewater-flow information at a fine spatiotemporal scale. The study develops and compares two AI-based models — an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) and a multilayer perceptron neural network (MLPNN) — to identify potential inflow and infiltration in the subcatchments of two pumping stations, using data gathered through a SCADA system.
46.methods: The study area is the city of Espoo, Finland, whose sewer network is more than 900 km long and contains approximately 200 pumping stations; two pumping stations were selected and their subcatchments delineated using a watershed algorithm. Rainfall was taken from radar rather than gauges, because Espoo has only two rain gauge sites while radar measurements cover all study catchments — specifically the Vantaa C-band dual-polarisation radar operated by the Finnish Meteorological Institute. Three rainfall-threshold values were defined from FMI definitions, under which a dry day has less than 0.3 mm/day and a rainy day between 1 and 4.4 mm/day, giving thresholds of 0.3, 1 and 2 mm/day; each was divided by 24 to obtain an estimated hourly rainfall value. For each pumping station the flow dataset was split into dry-day and wet-day sets against each threshold, with data below the threshold forming the dry-weather set and the remainder the wet-weather set, then normalised and used for both models. Flow data for typical weekdays were used so that water-consumption behaviour in the study area stayed comparable. Both models were evaluated with RMSE and the coefficient of determination R², and a sensitivity analysis was run by varying the rainfall threshold. Infiltration was identified by examining the normalised minimal dry weather flow of each subcatchment.
46.scope: Subcatchment-scale I/I identification for two sanitary sewer pumping stations in Espoo, using hourly SCADA flow and adjusted weather-radar rainfall. The stated purpose is to support spatial decision making in sewer system maintenance. Out of scope: sensor placement, hydraulic simulation, structural condition assessment, and any per-pipe attribution of the inferred I/I.
46.usefulness: Two things here are useful to us and neither is the model comparison. The first is the radar substitution: with only two rain gauges in a city, the authors switched to C-band dual-polarisation radar so that every study catchment had rainfall coverage. Any I/I or RDII analysis we attempt for an Adelaide catchment will hit the same gauge-density problem, and this is a documented precedent for solving it with an existing public data product rather than new instrumentation. The second is the diagnostic itself: normalised minimal dry weather flow above zero indicates that minimum dry weather flow exceeds what water consumption alone would produce, and therefore that infiltration is present. That is an infiltration screen computable from flow monitoring a utility already has, needs no rainfall data at all, and would let us rank subcatchments before deciding where to place anything. Together with Wang et al. (2024), it gives us two independent, cheap I/I indicators — minimum dry weather flow level and post-storm recovery time — that could feed a risk layer in a placement objective. The paper also usefully rules out a confounder: analysis showed water consumption from April to June and July to September was only about 1.2% and 0.4% below the whole-year average, indicating annual variation in water consumption has little effect on sewer base flow.
46.limitations: Both models were insensitive to the rainfall threshold in the dry-weather scenario but sensitive in the wet-weather scenario, because the wet-weather dataset contained far fewer data points, so raising the threshold shrank the rain data rapidly and made results threshold-dependent; the MLPNN was the more sensitive of the two for Station 2. The authors also note that if there are no existing data points to calibrate the random initial value, results can fall far from the expected value and generate excessive fluctuation. They state directly that the flow data are not yet sufficient for quantification of I/I in all situations, and that only after data quality improves will there be a better chance of estimating the network's response to individual rainfall events — which is a significant qualification on what the paper can claim. The two subcatchments were relatively small, so travel time from the farthest reach to the pumping station was on the order of minutes and flow delay could be ignored; that assumption will not hold for larger catchments. Beyond what is stated: only two pumping stations from a network of roughly 200 were studied; the analysis is hourly rather than fine-grained despite the stated need for fine spatiotemporal information; and no attempt is made to distinguish inflow from infiltration by mechanism or to locate the defects responsible.
46.conclusions: Both AI models produced similar inflow and infiltration patterns and both subcatchments were found to experience inflow and infiltration, with Subcatchment 1 showing the higher inflow level. The ANFIS model had overall higher performance than the MLPNN for modelling the I/I situation. Using a different rainfall threshold only slightly affected the dry-weather curves but significantly affected the wet-weather ones. The infiltration finding rests on normalised minimal dry weather flows being above zero in both subcatchments, again more so in Subcatchment 1, and the authors recommend further study of Subcatchment 1 to identify the causes of its high inflow and infiltration. The diurnal pattern was consistent with domestic use: minimum flow around 03:00, a rapid rise to a peak near 07:00 and a second peak near 20:00.
46.reflection: The honest assessment is that the ANFIS-versus-MLPNN comparison is the least interesting part of this paper and I would not build anything on it — with two stations and a small wet-weather sample, the performance ordering is not a result I would trust to generalise. What I would take is the workflow: delineate subcatchments with a watershed algorithm, pull radar rainfall where gauges are sparse, split by rainfall threshold, and use minimum dry weather flow as the infiltration screen. That is reproducible with public data and existing SCADA, and it is the kind of preliminary analysis that could justify where to instrument next. It also reinforces something the Sydney Water and Ningbo papers both suggest: a lot of useful monitoring intelligence is already sitting in pumping-station data that utilities have kept for years, and our project may add more value by showing how to read it than by proposing new hardware.
